replying_to: Replying to Spatial Frequency Bias in Convolutional Generative Adversarial Networks
display_title: Interesting idea but badly designed experiments

content.title: Interesting idea but badly designed experiments
content.review:
The paper looks into the inductive bias in generative networks that makes it easier for them to learn to output low frequencies than high frequencies. No completely satisfactory explanation to this apparent bias has been given so far. In this paper, both theoretical and experimental evidence is proposed for explaining this phenomenon, and an architecture is proposed to circumvent the bias.

The FID Levels measurement would benefit from further analysis. FID is based on a latent space of a network trained for classification, so any frequency biases of this classification network would be inherited by the FID metric itself. Hence its capability to resolve differences may vary between frequency bands for this reason alone. This effect should be somehow quantified before FID Levels can be considered a reliable metric.

My main concern about the paper is that the frequency shifting tests are so extreme. The construction of the high-frequency datasets in Section 3.2 effectively multiplies the images by a pixel-sized checkerboard of +1 and -1 values. The inability of GANs to reproduce such images is not at all surprising, because they are extremely unnatural and thus difficult to handle with  convolutional networks. I suppose this is partially the paper's point, but it would need to be shown with images that are not so extremely corrupted.

Even worse, the FSG experiment in Table 2 uses parameters that are exactly the same as were used for frequency-shifting the datasets. In effect, the GAN is tasked to generate the original, natural image, which is then frequency-shifted, i.e., multiplied by a checkerboard, afterwards according to Eq. 8. As such, the GAN objective ends up being the same as in the vanilla case with unmodified data and unmodified generator. The chosen shift parameters of $(\hat{u}_t,\hat{v}_t) = (\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})$ cause the weights of $G_i$ in Eq. 8 to be zero (the weight simplifies to $sin(\pi(x+y))$ which is identically zero for integer values of $x$ and $y$), and the weights of $G_r$ to be the checkerboard. The discriminator still has a harder time deciding between real and generated images when data is frequency-shifted, which probably explains why the results do not match exactly with the results in Table 1 with normal generators and non-shifted data - although with WGAN-GP they are very close.

Further experiments in Table 4 show some improvement in FID thanks to using an ensemble of FSGs, which is a compelling result. I would still like to see an improvement to a state-of-the-art FID using a modern dataset like FFHQ or CelebA-HQ, which should be possible to obtain if the method addresses a real issue. The original CelebA dataset is more of a curiosity these days, and known to exhibit various artifacts due to bad resizing operations and low-quality source material. More importantly, the observed improvements are questionable because the baseline FIDs in Table 1 do not agree with previously published results. Karras et al. 2019 (IEEE TPAMI) shows FIDs of 2.65 and 6.81 for StyleGAN and PG-GAN, respectively, whereas the corresponding results in Table 1 are 22.49 and 36.65 for StyleGAN2 and PG-GAN. These are quite large discrepancies and raise a question if the networks were trained properly.

To summarize, I find the experimental results too inconclusive to properly bring to light the effects of the frequency bias, or to provide solutions to it. Unless I have misunderstood the experiment in Section 4 completely, it is a bizarre setup where the generator's optimum is restored to exactly where it was, and the extra imaginary term can be neglected. I don't see any merit in this experiment, and even with the additional experiments I am not convinced that FSGs are a good way to combat the bias, because the paper has baseline results that are far from what the used networks should achieve.

Pros: important topic, nicely illustrated observation in Figure 1, an interesting although not properly analyzed idea for a frequency band specific distribution measure

Cons: badly designed experiments, use of archaic CelebA dataset

content.title: On why and how the experiments sufficiently support the claims
content.comment:
Thank you for reading and reviewing our work. We appreciate your feedback. We hope we can address your main concerns below:

1- We have provided True FID Levels on both datasets to show that the FID metric itself does not show any significant inherent bias over frequency bands, and this forms a baseline for comparison to GANs FID Levels. Please see the blue curve in Figure 1.

2- Please note that there is nothing “extreme” or “unnatural” about the frequency shifted images as far as the theories of CNNs and GANs are concerned. To the best of our knowledge, these theories do not provide any explicit reason for why generating a pattern of alternating +1s and -1s must be any harder than a constant pattern of +1s, so in our opinion it was actually quite surprising that the GANs cannot generate checkered patterns as well as non-checkered patterns! This is a solid empirical support for the existence of a spatial frequency bias. Please let us know if you have a specific reason that makes this unsurprising and expected in your view a priori.

3- In Table 2, the generator is not “tasked with generating the natural images”, we add a single shift layer to the generator, and then train it on the shifted images, and show that this shift layer is enough to improve the performance of GANs on the shifted images. This is surprising and interesting in three ways: first, this shows that the generative CNN is biased, otherwise adding this shift would not make any difference (an unbiased generative CNN must have been able to create such a shift layer by its own CNN filters). Second, this shows that the discriminative CNN can effectively learn high frequencies while the generative CNN can’t. Third, this shows that the bias in GANs can be effectively manipulated. Please note that none of these conclusions is a given without the experiments in Table 2.

4- Please note that our goal in this work is not to solve the bias, neither to improve the state-of-the-art, we are trying to expose a certain issue in CNN-GANs and investigate its roots. For this goal, we think the provided experiments are conclusive enough. FSG is not proposed as a solution to the bias, it is part of our investigation into the behavior of this bias and how it can be manipulated to match any known biases in the datasets. As we explain in Section 3.3, it is always possible to avoid this bias by training large models on high resolution images where the inherent high frequencies are diminished, this is what happens if using natural images at 1024x1024 resolution, and so we do all our tests on images of size 128x128 so that there is enough high frequency content left to expose the bias. The difference between FIDs and the state-of-the-art is because we are training the respective models on smaller images using smaller filter channel sizes, as mentioned in Section 3 (random samples from each model, the exact architecture, and the training conditions are provided in Appendix). But note that we are always comparing our models with themselves under the same training conditions (for example the same model is trained on shifted vs. unshifted image). Also, in Figure 1, we train the full-size StyleGAN2 on the 1024x1024 fractal, where high frequencies are not diminished, to confirm that the bias still persists even when training much larger models on much larger images, as long as those images do have high significant frequency content.

content.title: Clarification required
content.comment:
2- The convolutional networks' inductive bias towards natural images has been well established experimentally. The paper already cites Deep Image Priors where this inductive bias is used for corruption removal and inpainting. A followup by Gandelsman et al. (https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.00467) relies entirely on CNNs' preference towards generating natural images. Specific to GANs, it is known that the spectra of generated images is quite different from real images. Zhang et al. (https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.06515) show attenuated high frequencies in their own GAN model, and Wang et al. (https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.11035) compare multiple GAN architectures and observe that for most of them, their output spectra differs considerably from real images at high frequencies. There are large differences between different architectures, though, so findings cannot be generalized between them. The visualized spectra for ProGAN and StyleGAN in Figure 7 in Wang et al. anticipate results in Table 1 of the submission: StyleGAN's output is way off at high frequencies (indicating a failure to reproduce reference data there reliably), while ProGAN is much more consistent.

3- Maybe I'm not following Section 4 correctly, so please help me understand better. I interpret Eq. 6 so that $G$ is the output of a traditional, non-shifted generator, and the spatially varying multiplicative term introduces the frequency shift. In Eq. 8 the left-hand side is the final frequency-shifted output, and the right-hand side is a weighted (with spatially changing weights) sum of two non-shifted generators $G_r$ and $G_i$. Hence, given that the shift parameters are both $\frac{1}{2}$, it follows that $G_i$ is ignored as its multiplicative weights are zero, and the final frequency-shifted image is just the output of $G_r$ multiplied by the checkerboard pattern. Because the training data consists of images multiplied by the same checkerboard pattern, $G_r$ has to learn to generate traditional, non-shifted images, i.e., it has the same objective as in the usual setup where training data is not frequency shifted and there is no frequency shift layer in the network. If so, it is not surprising at all that the performance is restored close to the traditional setup with no frequency shifts anywhere. Please clarify where I'm mistaken here.

content.title: Clarification
content.comment:
2- In our previous comment, we were trying to point out that there is nothing unnatural or extreme about shifted images “as far as the theories are concerned”, not that it has never been observed that CNNs have issues with high frequencies. In the related works section, we discuss the recent observation of discrepancies between real and generated images in high frequencies, similar to the observations you referenced, but these discrepancies are neither tied to a consistent theoretical reason, nor to a systemic bias against learning high frequencies. Our paper provides a theoretical backbone for why such discrepancies happen and why they are the signs of a deeper systemic bias (please note that the up-sampling aliasing suggested as the theoretical cause of high frequency discrepancies in a few recent works, is not consistent with the observation that CNN-GANs still exhibit such discrepancies even when using a low-pass filter after the up-sampling operator to explicitly remove aliasing, e.g. in Dzanic & Witherden 2019 or Wang et al. 2020, in contrast, we argue that the problem is not that the up-sampling causes aliasing, but that the proceeding Conv filters cannot effectively transform/remove such aliased power). The overall point we are trying to communicate is that we think our paper unifies the recent spectral observations about CNNs and GANs under the notion of a spatial frequency bias, and improves the understanding of why such discrepancies happen and what are the overreaching consequences beyond causing high frequency artifacts that can be easily removed in post-processing (see how they are removed in Dzanic & Witherden, 2019 as a post-processing step).

3- We agree with your explanation, except for one part: “i.e., it has the same objective as in the usual setup where training data is not frequency shifted and there is no frequency shift layer in the network”. What you are referring to is that we (as human observers) know that *if* the generator preceding the shift layer simply generated the un-shifted natural images, then, given the shift layer on top of the generator, it would succeed in generating the shifted natural images. However, notice that this does not mean that the generator is “tasked” with generating the un-shifted images. The generator is “tasked” with reducing its loss on the loss surface formed by the discriminator on the space of shifted images. If adding a single shift layer on top of the generator enables it to perform better at this task, the logical conclusion is that the generator without such a layer had some limitations. To further clarify why this matters, assume we did not have Section 4 in the paper, then see if the following questions could have any sensible answer: 1. Is the bias due to the limitations in the discriminator or the generator (maybe the performance drop on shifted images is because the discriminator is not able to learn discriminative features from the shifted images, and therefore cannot provide any useful gradient to the generator, how can we know that the results in Section 3.2 is actually a bias rooted in the generative CNN)? 2. How can we know that the dataset of shifted images is not disrupting the optimization mechanism in some unpredictable way (how can we know that it is actually an architectural problem and not that shifting images breaks something in the optimization mechanism)? The results of Section 4 answer these questions, by showing how the bias can be effectively manipulated by *only* changing the generator's inner architecture (i.e. adding a shift-layer on top of the generative CNN).

display_title: An interesting exploration but left with more questions than answers

content.title: An interesting exploration but left with more questions than answers
content.review:
**Summary**: This paper examines the ability of GANs to learn distributions outside the typical natural image distributions for which they were originally developed. Specifically, the authors scrutinize the ability of GANs to model high frequencies, which are more scarce than low frequencies in natural image data. The authors provide evidence that GANs may be biased against producing high frequencies, and propose a solution to ensemble several GANs to (implicitly) model different frequency bands.

Overall, I agree with the authors that the sensitivity of GANs to different frequency bands in data merits scrutiny. Additionally, the paper is well-written and reasonably clear. However, I feel that this paper unfortunately leaves me with more questions than answers. A few of them follow, in descending order of my perceived importance.

*Why are the motivating applications not considered?* The motivation for this work is strong and clear: despite being designed for natural images, GANs are increasingly employed to generate data from other distributions such as medical data (Kazuhiro et al. 2018), satellite images (Ganguli et al. 2019), waveforms (Donahue et al. 2019), seismic data (Wang et al. 2019), etc., where high-frequency information may be vital. Despite this nice motivation, the authors choose to examine only artificial datasets consisting of frequency-shifted images. It makes sense to look at such data for initial experimentation, but it doesn't make sense to state the aforementioned motivation and never examine anything besides (manipulated) natural images.

*Why blame GANs and not generative ConvNets?* I take issue with one particular aspect of the narrative: that the bias against high frequencies is attributed to "GANs" and not "convolution-based generative image models". In fact, there is no experiment in this paper which looks at the culpability of the GAN _learning algorithm_; only the architecture (convnets). There are two reasons this is problematic:
1. The _inattentive_ reader is left with the impression that the learning algorithm rather than the architecture is to blame
1. The _attentive_ reader is left wondering if the learning algorithm _should_ be to blame, or if it is exclusively an architectural problem

*Can we _fix_ the inductive bias instead of hacking together a solution?* I think the frequency-shifted GAN idea is cute. It makes perfect sense on paper: GANs seemed to be biased towards a particular band (low frequencies), so let's just artificially shift other frequencies into this band as a pre-processing step, and merge the outputs of a "bank" (as in filter bank) of GANs which specialize in different bands. However, this strikes me as a hack and not something that we (as a research community) actually want to be doing down the road. Why not take a closer look at the inductive bias (convnets) and see what we can do about eliminating their bias against high frequencies while preserving their ability to effectively model lower frequencies?

*Is the frequency-shifted GAN actually working?* In Figure 4, the "shape" of the scores from the frequency-shifted GAN matches that of the corresponding standard GAN. Why is that? Is it possible the improved performance is just coming from the additional capacity? Seems like you could run the same experiment without the frequency shifting inductive bias to ablate.

*What of our metrics?* There is a small amount of discussion about metrics at the end of Section 5, but I would like to see more explanation of the bias of our *metrics* to different frequency bands.

*What about high-frequency artifacts?* GANs (especially earlier convolutional GANs) are known to generate undesirable high-frequency artifacts, commonly referred to as _checkerboard_ artifacts (Odena et al. 2016). I find it difficult to reconcile the existence of these artifacts with the theoretical framework expressed in this paper. Can the authors clarify what these artifacts imply w.r.t. their hypotheses?

Low-level detail(s):
- I like the thought experiment in paragraph 1. So much that I would love to see it move from thought experiment to toy example :)
- Axes are too small to be readable in Figures 3 and 4
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection

display_title: The nature of this work is to raise questions about GANs, and the experiments are designed to unambiguously and sufficiently support the validity of these questions

content.title: The nature of this work is to raise questions about GANs, and the experiments are designed to unambiguously and sufficiently support the validity of these questions
content.comment:
Thank you for reading and reviewing our work. We appreciate your helpful feedback and insightful questions. We hope we can clarify some of your questions below:

1- Please note that our main objective in this work is to study the *existence* of the spatial frequency bias in CNN-GANs and its roots (and not to provide a solution to this bias, please see below about FSG), and as such, we designed experiments that can directly and unambiguously support this objective. We chose CelebA and LSUN-Bedrooms because we wanted to study the bias on datasets for which these models are originally designed. We also connect our discussion to the real-world applications in the fractal experiment displayed in Figure 1 (since most real-world data follow some sort of a fractal pattern, this directly illustrates the overreaching effects of this bias). We agree that experiments on real-world applications would be an interesting addition, but we don’t see why lack of such experiments would hurt the main claims of this paper.

2- We try to clarify this distinction in the introduction ("In this work, we first mathematically reveal a spectral bias in the structure of generative convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and then empirically show its manifestation into a spatial frequency bias in GANs”). So while we do not theoretically tie the bias to the adversarial training, we are still relying on the GAN framework to expose this bias empirically, and therefore we can not argue that the adversarial training plays no part in the observed bias, we slightly touch on this in the discussion (“We also observed [Section 4] that the spatial frequency bias primarily affects GAN's generator and not its discriminator. This gives the discriminator an advantage which can be the root of certain instabilities in GAN training”). We agree that ideally one would like a nice clean statement like “generative CNNs have structural bias!” but to support this empirically, one has to train generative CNNs in some framework, and that will inevitably tie the observations to the inherent limitations in that framework, resulting in a less ideal statement like “generative CNNs have structural bias in GANs/VAEs/AEs/etc!”. We also touch on why we study CNNs in GANs and not some other generative models in the related works (“In theory, GANs must be able to learn any suitable distribution regardless of the carrier spatial frequencies. Therefore, while a systemic spectral bias in generative CNNs could be obscured by the inherent spectral biases of AEs, VAEs and L2 tasks, the GANs provide a clear lens for observing such biases”).

3- Yes, FSG is indeed not a proper solution to the frequency bias. FSG is meant as a contribution to the main story of the paper which is to study the existence of the spatial frequency bias and its roots. It’s main purpose is to expose certain behaviors of the bias, and to show how this bias can be manipulated to match the known biases of a dataset.

4- FSG does actually work, as per the results in Table 2 (if the shift was not effective, we would not see any improvement). Multiple-FSGs do have an increased capacity, but using different frequency shift targets for the FSGs results in different performance gains (1/16 was the target frequency that resulted in the best performance on CelebA in our preliminary tests), so the added capacity alone is not causing the improvement and the shift matters, as expected from Table 2.

5- We have tried to show the bias of the FID Levels to different frequency bands using True FID Levels, which works as a baseline to FID Levels of GANs.

6- The checkerboard artifacts can be thought of as the failure of the conv-filter to effectively transform/remove aliasing caused by its preceding upsampling operator (one can think of each conv layer as receiving an spectrum filled with aliasing artifacts -- due to the upsampling -- which it must filter/carve-out to reach at its desired spectrum). Theorem 1 explains the reason for this failure. Intuitively, Theorem 1 implies that the conv-filter that is primarily responsible for generating high frequencies cannot freely “carve-out” its input spectrum (due to correlations in the conv-filter spectrum). For example, if the conv-filter wants to amplify/diminish a specific high frequency component of the input, it cannot achieve this without changing nearby components as well, and this could be framed as generating artifacts, or equivalently failure to remove artifacts. Also, note that modern GANs use a fixed low-pass filter after upsampling (e.g. nearest neighbor or bilinear) to reduce such artifacts manually. Nevertheless, we show that the underlying cause, namely correlation in conv-filters, still remains and has real effects.

7- Section 3.2 is essentially the thought experiment in paragraph 1: we train GANs on the same image distribution with and without shifting the frequencies. Axes fonts are fixed now.

display_title: Interesting viewpoint, but theory and experiments leave too many questions

content.title: Interesting viewpoint, but theory and experiments leave too many questions
content.review:
The paper argues that CNN's have a built-in bias that makes them more adept at generating low frequency than high frequency content. This is an interesting hypothesis that is worthy of studying, however I am not quite convinced by the reasoning and experiments in the paper.

First, about the theory.

Overall the math notation is somewhat confusing, and does not do what notation ideally does, which is to unambiguously clarify what is meant in the text. I'll mention this on a couple of occassions below. 

It appears that a key assumption is made that CNN's can be studied as linear functions. The argument is that ReLU nonlinearities are locally linear. I am rather skeptical about whether this is valid in this context, and whether dropping the relus in Eq. 3 is mathematically valid. It is not clear what is meant by "neighborhood of H^1" or "locality of any single sample". When linearizing, one obtains a first-order Taylor expansion, which contains the original formula (relus and all) evaluated at a fixed point, and then a linear perturbation that's based on the derivative at that point (but generally does not correspond to a sequence of linear layers). This function will indeed be linear in the perturbation, but it is certainly not the function in Eq. 3 where the relus are simply dropped. In more practical terms, imagine taking a trained neural network and then dropping all the relus from it. The result is not a "linearized network" but rather a network that returns completely arbitrary results and has little relation to the original one. 

This is not just a question of whether the formal notation is correct, but to me it calls to question whether the overall reasoning ignores some critically important factors. I can buy the argument that a _linear_ CNN suffers from this kind of a bias, for the reasons stated in the paper, but linear networks are extremely poor generators for a variety of reasons, and hardly relevant in practice. I suspect that the nonlinearities play a key role in shaping the spectrum, and this is ignored by the analysis. For example, imagine something as simple as a spatial sine wave before and after applying a relu on it. The spectra are completely different and such effects likely have significant consequences on how the spectrum is built by the network.

The notation about absorbing the upsampling operator seems questionable. As far as I see it could be absorebed into the convolution kernel with suitable care. But doing it this way is basically just saying that the operation is still secretly done somewhere, but now the notation no longer describes it, which is not very helpful.

As for the overall thesis, I do find it plausible that CNN's do better with low frequencies, but I am not fully convinced that these derivations are the fundamental reason for such behavior.

Experiments.

I am also somewhat skeptical about whether the experiments support the conclusions of the paper, at least as strongly as suggested.

For the FID experiments, a potential problem is that the metric is not comparable between different datasets. For example good performance on FFHQ results in different FID values than good performance on CelebA, and the performance in these datasets cannot be meaningfully compared based on these values. Similarly, it might be that the change of FID in figure 3 is mostly explained by the underlying datasets being different at each point in the x-axis, due to the drastically changed image content in the training data. One possible way to study this would be to show a baseline where a subset of e.g. FFHQ is compared by FID to another disjoint subset of FFHQ (simulating a "perfect" learning result), and seeing whether the curve stays flat as a function of the high pass (as is implicitly assumed in the paper now).

As for the high-frequency shifting experiments, I like some parts of the reasoning behind it in principle. However given all the reservations about the analysis above, I am not sure if there is a strong logical connection between the paper's arguments and the results of this experiment. In the end it boils down to multiplying all images in the dataset by a single-pixel-pitch checkerboard pattern, which is unnatural for most CNNs for any number of reasons (though this heavily depends on design details of the final layers) regardless of its spectral interpretation.

Finally, the proposed FSG architecture. 

First of all, the vastly improved results for 0.5-frequency shift (changing DC to Nyquist) seem unsurprising when the data is similarly spectrum-shifted. This again boils down to manually multiplying the generated image by a checkerboard image before feeding it to the generator. The layers of the generator are then unaware of the the need to draw a checkerboard, and do what they always do. The task of the discriminator is marginally harder than before, effectively it just needs to learn to remove the checerboard in the first layer, which is easy with convolutions. So almost nothing changes from the usual case of "clean" data, and training goes well. So problem solved? Unfortunately the setup is extremely contrived, and not applicable to any dataset that wasn't multiplied with a checkerboard pattern -- indeed, applying this particular FSG-shift with any regular dataset would probably degrade the results greatly, like in the shifted-data experiments.

The somewhat more interesting variant is where less drastic shifts are made. It's interesting (if not overtly surprising) to see that the network learns to naturally latch onto the easiest way available to generate the particular frequencies. This could have some potential for further study and development. At the moment its usefulness is limited by the fact that the shifts are specified as fixed hyperparameters that are probably dataset-specific. Would there be sense in learning them on the fly instead? The argument that there is no increase in computational resources is also questionable in this case, as additional layers are introduced. The paper currently keeps these low-capacity, but one has to wonder if insisting on keeping them low capacity limits the quality of the results.

In summary, I think the authors are right to be studying questions like this, but in the present form of the paper, I am not enough convinced about the reasoning or the experiments to recommend acceptance.

_POST-REBUTTAL UPDATE_

I unfortunately missed the time window to discuss the authors' response further with them, but I still wish to address the linearization issue. I believe we agree up to a certain point, and I realize my explanation above was not the clearest. The existence of _some_ linear (well, affine) function around a point is indeed what I mean by the Taylor expansion. However, what I do not agree on is that such linear functions could be expressed as a CNN in general, because _convolutionality_ is a strong restriction on the space of linear functions. Quite simply, there is no guarantee that this locally linear piece could be expressed as a linear CNN of a given architecture with _any_ choice of weights -- indeed, I suspect vast majority could not, and those that can might need to use extremely contrived filters. With a full linear MLP instead of CNN they could of course -- that would simply be the Taylor expansion (that is, full linear + bias). For this reason I believe that the reasoning is not quite valid.

My bad for missing the True FID levels, this does indeed make the experiment somewhat more relevant. However, my overall opinion remains that there are too many issues to recommend acceptance at this time.

content.title: Clarifying why and how the experiments support the theory
content.comment:
Thank you for reading and reviewing our work. We appreciate your feedback. We hope we can address your main concerns below:

1- Please note that we are not simply dropping ReLUs from a CNN and saying that the resulting network is equivalent, this is obviously wrong as you pointed out, we are saying that there *exists* an equivalent linear CNN at the neighborhood of any input (locality of any sample: imagine we pick any one point from the input space of a CNN, and only consider how well the network generates samples when the input is only coming from a small neighborhood of this point, that is, a small perturbation of this point). Since all operations in generative ReLU-CNNs are either linear or piecewise-linear, the entire network will have a piecewise linear output space, and the existence of a linear equivalent CNN at the locality of each sample is a direct consequence of piecewise linearity. Please also note how the prediction of Theorem 1 are empirically evaluated on the filters of a *trained* WGAN in Figure 2.

2- Our thinking was that adding a new variable like $T^l=Up(H^l)$ and then rewriting the Conv layer using $T$ might become too tedious to read, and we assumed just saying “Up is absorbed in H” would imply this change of variable. However, we agree that this might be confusing. We have modified the paper to clarify this point (see the leading lines to Equation 3).

3- You mentioned “one possible way to study this would be to show a baseline where a subset of e.g. FFHQ is compared by FID to another disjoint subset of FFHQ”, we do exactly that on both CelebA and LSUN-Bedrooms to provide a baseline for comparison, it is called True FID Levels in the paper and it does stay approximately flat compared to GANs FID Levels. Please see section 3.1 and the blue curves in Figure 3. 

4- Yes, the frequency shift boils down to that checkered-pattern multiplication. But what that multiplication is doing is swapping high and low spatial frequencies of images, and as far as we know, neither CNNs nor GANs theory mention any limitation based on the spatial frequency contents of the data, that is, while these "checkered" images would be unnatural for us as humans (unnatural in the sense that our eyes are not accustomed to see such images around us), they are by no means unnatural for CNN-GANs as far as the theories are concerned. So, if we discover that such a multiplication indeed disrupts the performance of GANs, as we do in Section 3.2, it is a clear sign that there is a certain spatial frequency limitation.

5- In FSG, we add a single shift layer to the generator, and show that this shift layer is enough to improve the performance of GANs on shifted data. This is surprising and interesting in three ways: first, this shows that the generative CNN is biased, otherwise adding this shift would not make any difference (an unbiased generative CNN should have been able to create such a shift layer by its own CNN filters). Second, this shows that the discriminative CNN can effectively learn high frequencies while the generative CNN can’t. Third, this shows that the bias in GANs can be effectively manipulated. Please note that none of these conclusions is a given without the experiments in Table 2. You have mentioned that you think it is easy for the CNN to learn to remove the checkered pattern, however this is not a given, it needs empirical proof, and that is what FSG provides. If you think it is easy for the discriminative CNN to remove a checkered pattern (high frequency), why do you not think the same of a generative CNN (to be able to generate a checkered pattern)? This question is what our paper is all about, and FSG is meant as a way to show that this bias not only exists, but can be manipulated. Please note that we do not suggest that FSG solves the bias, we suggest it as a way to match the spatial bias of GANs to the known spatial biases of a dataset.

content.title: Review of Spatial Frequency Bias in Convolutional Generative Adversarial Networks
content.review:
This work aims at highlighting a spatial frequency biais in convolutional GANs, and proposes FSG, a method to circumvent this bias. More specifically, it states that high frequencies in a generative convolution architecture are harder to produce as the higher the frequency, the more correlation there is between adjacent frequencies, making it difficult for the network to adjust to specific high frequencies in the data without affecting adjacent ones. This is shown both theoretically and empirically, and is corroborated by experiments that highlight the fact that GANs yield larger errors on the higher frequencies. To overcome this issue, they propose to learn generators whose frequencies are shifted around specific high frequencies. 

The attacked problem is interesting and the research questions have potential implications in various scientific fields where GANs are applied.

The paper is written clearly and reads well. The experimental analysis is interesting and seems to be conducted rigorously. If shifting the frequencies does not hinder the GAN training and introduce additional instabilities, shifting the frequencies as proposed in the paper could be a useful ‘hack’ for specific problems.

However, up to the best of my understanding, the theoretical results seem a little unrelated with the narrative. The paper states that it is difficult for the network to adjust itself to high frequencies, a consequence of the high correlation between adjacent frequencies. However, correlation is computed with respect to the randomness due from different initialisations (this is what I have understood reading in between the lines in the proof, but should be clearly stated in the assumptions, see below). A priori, this correlation during initialisation is by no means linked to the difficulty to adjust the network, which is a dynamic property that should hold at all times. If there indeed is a link, I suggest the authors make it explicit. In the contrary, a different quantity should be considered, e.g. a measure of the impact of a small perturbation applied to a high frequency of the output with respect to adjacent frequencies would better correspond to the narrative. This is for me the main issue that should be addressed.

The independence assumption of the unrestricted filter component G, for the spatial frequency components only seems to hold during initialization. As a consequence, Thm 1 only applies during initialization. If this is the case, this should be clearly stated.


It would have been interesting to propose a real world application where this work, specifically FSGs could be motivated, or at least state specific cases where modifying a prior on the frequencies could be useful. 

How exactly are the multiple FSGs combined? Are these trained jointly? Additional details are needed.

content.title: On the link between the theorem and the narrative
content.comment:
Thank you for reading and reviewing our work. We appreciate your feedback on the theory, we hope we can clarify what the theorem means and how it links to a spectral limitation below:

1- The correlation in Theorem 1 is defined over the probability space of all possible 2D Conv filters of a specific filter size and a specific output dimension. To hopefully make this more clear, imagine we have in our hand any 2D filter with the specified sizes, and then we decide to increase/decrease the value of a specific component in its spectrum -- to amplify/diminish a certain frequency component of the input. Theorem 1 tells us that if we change the value of this component, we will observe changes in the other components as well, because it shows that in the space of all such 2D filters, whenever that certain component is increased/decreased, certain other components change with it as well.

2- Regarding the independence assumption on G in the proof, it holds throughout the training by definition. G, as a random variable, is *defined* over the space of all 2D filters that can independently adjust their spectrum. Any 2D filter that a layer of any generative CNN would be able to form at any point during training would be one point on this space (iid initialization is important to make sure that the “ideal” generative CNNs are not restricted to a specific subspace of this space). Essentially, G is a mathematical trick to illustrate the limitation of F that is being used in CNNs in practice: we are assuming an ideal G that can freely adjust any location on its spectrum, and then study how restricting this G in a certain way to reach F would affect this freedom. Please also notice how in Figure 2 (Left), we are evaluating the predictions of the theorem on the “trained” WGAN, not the initialized network. We have modified the proof to clarify these points, and have also dropped an unnecessary symmetric assumption on the pulse function. Please see the proof and the theorem statement for changes.

3- Multiple FSGs are added to the main generator and are trained jointly (they form a single generative network). However, please note that the main objective of this work is to show the existence of a spatial frequency bias in GANs and to investigate its roots, and FSG is meant primarily as part of that objective, as a way to understand the behavior of this bias (and how it can be manipulated), not as a proper solution to this bias, although it can be used as an easy trick to match the biases of GANs to the known biases of a dataset.
